title: Duty of candour: explaining a retained swab

header.contentArea: Communication skills in giving and receiving information and history taking
guidelineVersions: GMC/NMC Openness and honesty when things go wrong (2015; updated Dec 2024)
NHS England Never Events list 2018 (updated Feb 2021; still in use, May 2026)

related.id: MB-177 Angry relative after a delayed diagnosis

related.why: Consent for the return to theatre

brief.scenario: Mrs Joanne Pritchard, 52, is day 6 after an emergency laparotomy and repair of a perforated duodenal ulcer. She developed fever and abdominal pain yesterday. This morning's CT shows a retained surgical swab with a surrounding collection. Your consultant, who did the operation, plans a return to theatre this afternoon. She is finishing an emergency case and will join you in about 10 minutes. Mrs Pritchard has asked for her scan result.
brief.task: Explain the scan result to Mrs Pritchard and address her concerns.

beforeYouWalkIn.frame: Tell her plainly, say sorry, explain what happens next, and don't guess or blame.
beforeYouWalkIn.trap: Euphemisms ("something was seen"), or refusing to say sorry in case it admits liability.
beforeYouWalkIn.firstMove: Sit down, ask if she'd like someone with her, then give a warning shot.

grid.label: Preparation and setting
grid.fail: Starts in a shared bay, without knowing the facts or telling the consultant.
grid.pass: Knows the CT result and plan; private room; nurse present; offers a support person; consultant aware and joining.
grid.high: Checks what she already knows and whether she wants her husband there before starting.

grid.label: Clear disclosure
grid.fail: Uses euphemism ("a foreign body") or delays telling her.
grid.pass: Warning shot, then plain words: a swab was left inside after the first operation.
grid.high: Pauses after the disclosure, lets her react, and separates what is known from what isn't.

grid.label: Apology
grid.fail: Doesn't apologise, or says "I'm sorry you feel that way".
grid.pass: A sincere, personal apology for what happened.
grid.high: Says sorry is not an admission of legal liability; the apology covers what happened, the harm and preventing it again.

grid.label: Consequences and plan
grid.fail: Minimises the harm or gives no plan.
grid.pass: Explains the collection, antibiotics, and the operation today to remove the swab; the consultant will explain and seek consent.
grid.high: Is honest that recovery may take longer, and says what the operation involves in plain words.

grid.label: Questions without blame or speculation
grid.fail: Blames a colleague, or guesses how it happened.
grid.pass: Says he doesn't yet know how it happened and won't guess; it will be investigated.
grid.high: Doesn't take personal blame or blame others, and doesn't promise it could never happen to anyone again.

grid.label: Reporting and investigation
grid.fail: Doesn't report it, or says there will be no investigation.
grid.pass: Reports it as a patient safety incident; explains it is a Never Event and will be investigated; she'll be told the findings.
grid.high: Explains the team will review how it happened and what will change, and that she can be involved in the review.

grid.label: Statutory duty of candour
grid.fail: Doesn't know that the organisation must follow up.
grid.pass: Recognises a notifiable safety incident (moderate harm): in person, a true account and apology, then written notification.
grid.high: Explains why: significant, non-permanent harm needing an unplanned return to surgery is moderate harm; writing follows with findings and apology (reg 20(4)).

grid.label: Support, contact and record
grid.fail: Leaves with no contact point and no record.
grid.pass: Named contact; PALS; documents the conversation and the apology in the notes.
grid.high: Offers independent support (AvMA, Healthwatch) and asks what she needs now.

fail.speaker: candidate
fail.text: [At the bedside in the bay] Hi. The scan showed a foreign body, so you're going back to theatre.

fail.speaker: examiner
fail.text: Mrs Pritchard: “A foreign body? What does that mean?”

fail.speaker: candidate
fail.text: Something from the operation. It's minor. I can't say sorry, because it wasn't my fault.

fail.speaker: examiner
fail.text: Mrs Pritchard: “Whose fault was it, then?”

fail.speaker: candidate
fail.text: Probably the scrub nurse; they do the count.

fail.speaker: examiner
fail.text: Mrs Pritchard: “Will anyone look into this?”

fail.speaker: candidate
fail.text: Once you're better it won't matter. [Leaves without writing anything]

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: Hello, I'm Dr Rahman, one of the surgical trainees. Could we talk in here? Can I check your name? Would you like someone with you? The nurse will stay, and my consultant is joining us shortly.

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: I'm afraid the scan has shown something that should not have happened. During your first operation, a surgical swab was left inside your abdomen.

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: I am very sorry that this has happened to you.

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: There's infection around it, which is why you've had a fever. You're on antibiotics. You'll need an operation this afternoon to remove it; my consultant will explain it and ask for your consent.

pass.speaker: examiner
pass.text: Mrs Pritchard: “How could this happen? Who did it?”

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: I don't know yet, and I won't guess. It will be looked into properly.

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: I'll report it as a patient safety incident. It's what the NHS calls a Never Event, so it will be investigated, and you'll be told what's found.

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: Because this has harmed you and needs another operation, the hospital has a legal duty to meet you, explain what happened and apologise, then write to you.

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: The ward sister is your contact, and PALS can help too. I'll write down what we've discussed, including my apology, in your notes.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: Hello, I'm Dr Rahman, one of the surgical trainees. Could we talk in here? Can I check your name? Would you like your husband here, or on the phone? The nurse will stay, and my consultant, who did your operation, is joining us in a few minutes and will lead from there. What have you been told so far?

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: I'm afraid I have some difficult news. The scan shows that a surgical swab was left inside your abdomen at your first operation. [Pause] That's what we know. How it happened, we don't know yet.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: I am very sorry. Saying sorry isn't about legal blame; it's because this shouldn't have happened, and we will find out why and stop it happening again.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: There's an infection around the swab. The operation today opens the same wound, removes the swab and washes out the infection. Your recovery will probably take longer than planned, and I won't pretend otherwise.

high.speaker: examiner
high.text: Mrs Pritchard: “Was it the nurses? Can you promise this won't happen to anyone else?”

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: I won't blame anyone before the facts are known. I can't promise it will never happen again, but I can promise it will be looked into and changes made.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: It's reported today. The review will look at how the checks failed, and you can tell the team what you want answered.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: This has caused you harm that needs another operation, so the hospital has a legal duty of candour: it must meet you in person, explain what's known and apologise, then write to you with the findings and an apology.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: Action against Medical Accidents or Healthwatch can give independent advice. I'll record our conversation and my apology. What do you need right now?

failures.move: Calling it "a foreign body" or "something from the operation".
failures.consequence: She isn't told what happened, which breaches candour and destroys trust when she finds out.

failures.move: Refusing to apologise because it might admit liability.
failures.consequence: An apology is not of itself an admission of negligence in law, and she has a right to one.
Speculation before the facts; unfair to a colleague and possibly wrong.

failures.move: Not reporting because she will recover.
failures.consequence: Safety-critical: a Never Event goes uninvestigated, and the same failure can harm the next patient.

recovery.when: She asks if you're covering something up
recovery.line: No. I've told you everything we know so far, and you'll be told what the investigation finds.
That's your right. My apology stands, and I'll make sure you get the information you need.

knowledge.fact: Retained foreign object post procedure (including counted swabs) is a Never Event; the 2018 list remains in use while NHS England explores a new approach.
Speak as soon as possible, with a support person available; don't wait for the investigation (para 11). The lead clinician is usually most appropriate (para 10).
Notifiable safety incident: tell in person with a true account, enquiries and an apology, recorded; then in writing with the results (reg 20(3)–(4)).
An apology is not of itself an admission of negligence (s2).
Record Never Events on LFPSE; learning responses follow PSIRF.

recall.think: A Never Event: she is owed the truth and an apology.
recall.say: "A surgical swab was left inside you. I am very sorry."

numbers.meaning: parts of an apology: what happened, the harm, prevention

recall.finish: Consultant meets her; theatre; written follow-up.

sources.name: GMC and NMC: Openness and honesty when things go wrong: the professional duty of candour
sources.version: In effect 29 June 2015; last updated 13 December 2024
sources.supports: Tell the patient, apologise, offer a remedy or support, explain the short- and long-term effects; the most appropriate team member is usually the lead or accountable clinician (para 10); speak as soon as possible, with someone available to support the patient, without waiting for an investigation, clear about what is and is not established (para 11); share what is known, explain uncertainty, answer honestly (para 12); an apology covers what happened, what can be done about harm and what will prevent recurrence (para 14); apologising is not admitting legal liability (para 15); no personal responsibility for a colleague's mistake, but the patient has a right to an apology (para 16); personalised apology, named contact in the team, information about independent advocacy, counselling or other support services, and a record of the apology in the clinical record (para 17); report in England and Wales to LFPSE (para 25a)

sources.name: Health and Social Care Act 2008 (Regulated Activities) Regulations 2014 (SI 2014/2936), regulation 20: duty of candour
sources.supports: After a notifiable safety incident, notify the relevant person as soon as reasonably practicable and give reasonable support (20(2)); notification in person, with a true account of the facts known, the further enquiries planned, an apology, and a secure written record (20(3)); followed by a written notification including the results of further enquiries and an apology (20(4)); keep copies of correspondence (20(6)); moderate harm: significant, not permanent, harm needing a moderate increase in treatment, which includes an unplanned return to surgery (20(7)); for a health service body, a notifiable safety incident is unintended or unexpected and, in a health care professional's reasonable opinion, could result in or appears to have resulted in death, severe or moderate harm, or prolonged psychological harm (20(8))

sources.name: Compensation Act 2006 (c. 29), section 2
sources.supports: An apology, an offer of treatment or other redress, shall not of itself amount to an admission of negligence or breach of statutory duty (England and Wales)

sources.name: NHS England: Never Events list 2018
sources.version: First published January 2018; last updated February 2021
sources.supports: Never Event 3: retained foreign object post procedure, including items subject to a formal count such as swabs, needles, instruments and guidewires; national safety requirements include the WHO surgical safety checklist and NatSSIPs

sources.name: NHS England: Revised Never Events policy and framework (web page)
sources.supports: Never Events are wholly preventable where strong national systemic barriers exist; the framework remains in use while NHS England develops a replacement; Never Events are recorded on the Learn from Patient Safety Events (LFPSE) service, with learning responses in line with PSIRF

sources.name: NHS England: Patient Safety Incident Response Framework (PSIRF)
sources.supports: Replaces the Serious Incident Framework (2015); compassionate engagement and involvement of those affected by patient safety incidents is a core aim

sources.name: NHS England: Provisional publication of Never Events reported as occurring between April 2025 and March 2026
sources.supports: The existing Never Events framework and 2018 list remain in use during the discovery phase that followed the 2024 consultation (findings published 16 September 2025); retained foreign object post procedure is still reported as a Never Event (121 reported April 2025 to March 2026)

partner.opening: Mrs Pritchard is in the side room with a nurse. Please begin when you're ready.
partner.actorBrief: You are Joanne Pritchard, 52, a primary school teacher. Opening line: "Have you got my scan result? Nobody's telling me anything." Emotional state: anxious, then shocked, then angry. After the disclosure, go quiet for a moment, then ask: "How could you leave something inside me?" Calm a little if the candidate apologises sincerely and explains plainly. Get angrier with euphemism, blame of a colleague, or "I can't say sorry". Your husband is at work; if asked, you'd like him told and on the phone. Hidden concern, only if asked what worries you most: you are due to start a new job in three weeks and fear losing it. Ask: "Can you promise this won't happen to anyone else?" and, later, "I want a different surgeon."

reveals.finding: "They said the scan was to look for an infection."
"My husband, Steve. He's at work; can you ring him?"
"I start a new job in three weeks. Will I be well enough?"

reveals.trigger: Asks what she wants from the investigation
reveals.finding: "I want to know why the count didn't catch it."

push.question: Does the statutory duty of candour apply, and what does it require?
push.expect: Yes. In a clinician's reasonable opinion it has caused moderate harm (significant, non-permanent harm needing an unplanned return to surgery), so it is a notifiable safety incident: in person as soon as reasonably practicable, true account, planned enquiries, apology, recorded; then written notification with the findings and an apology.

push.question: Who should lead this conversation?
push.expect: Usually the lead or accountable clinician: here the consultant, who is joining and should lead the formal notification. She has asked for her result, so honest disclosure should not wait for the consultant or the investigation.

curveballs.prompt: "I want a different surgeon to do the operation."
curveballs.safeAnswer: Acknowledge it; tell the consultant straight away; the team will discuss who operates; don't promise what can't be arranged.
Acknowledge her right; the apology stands; offer AvMA for independent advice.

curveballs.prompt: "Can you promise this won't happen to anyone else?"
curveballs.safeAnswer: Can't promise; commits to the investigation and to sharing what changes.

curveballs.prompt: "I don't want the details, just get it out."
curveballs.safeAnswer: Respect it; explore why; record her wish; tell her she can ask for more at any time.
